title: Normal Approximations

blocks.title: When to Use a Normal Approximation to a Binomial
teacherCues: Ask: 'If a binomial experiment has n=150 and p=0.85, why is using the binomial formula for P(x<100) impractical?'
Write the conditions np ≥ 5 and nq ≥ 5 on the board. Emphasize these must both be true.

discoveryHook.scenario: Imagine a doctor performs a surgical procedure with an 85% success rate on 150 patients. Finding the probability of fewer than 100 successes using the binomial formula would require summing 100 individual probabilities—a tedious task. A normal approximation turns this into a simple z-score problem!

explanation: A binomial distribution can be approximated by a normal distribution when both $ n p \ge 5 $ and $ n q \ge 5 $.
If these conditions are met, the binomial random variable $x$ is approximately normally distributed.
The mean of the approximating normal distribution is $ \mu = n p $.
The standard deviation is $ \sigma = \sqrt{n p q} $, where $ q = 1 - p $.
This approximation works well when $n$ is large enough that the distribution appears bell-shaped.

formulaCard.title: Normal Approximation to Binomial
notes: Only valid if $ n p \ge 5 $ and $ n q \ge 5 $.

examples.title: A – Decide and Find Parameters
examples.prompt: Sixty-two percent of adults have an HDTV. You randomly select 45 adults and ask if they have an HDTV. Decide if you can use a normal approximation and find the mean and standard deviation.
steps: Both conditions met, so normal approximation is appropriate.

examples.title: B – Why Not Approximate?
examples.prompt: Twelve percent of adults without an HDTV plan to buy one. You randomly select 30 such adults. Decide if you can use a normal approximation and explain.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Which condition fails? Why does that matter?
steps: Since $np < 5$, the normal approximation is not appropriate; the distribution is too skewed.

examples.title: C – Planning to Buy 3D TV
examples.prompt: Five percent of adults plan to buy a 3D TV. You randomly select 125 adults. Decide if you can use a normal approximation and find the mean and standard deviation if so.

confusionCorner.title: Check Both np and nq
confusionCorner.body: Both $ n p \ge 5 $ and $ n q \ge 5 $ must be true. If either is below 5, the binomial distribution is too skewed for a normal approximation.

questions.prompt: To use a normal approximation to a binomial distribution, both $ n p $ and $ n q $ must be at least ___.
hints: It is the minimum threshold for each product.
The condition is often stated as $np \ge 5$ and $nq \ge 5$.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Both products must be at least 5.

questions.prompt: For a binomial experiment with $n=50$, $p=0.3$, what is the mean $\mu$?
If $n=20$, $p=0.85$, $q=0.15$, can you use a normal approximation? (yes/no)

blocks.title: Applying the Continuity Correction
teacherCues: Draw a binomial histogram bar centered at x = c. Shade the rectangle. Then overlay a normal curve and show the interval c−0.5 to c+0.5.
Ask: 'Why do we add or subtract 0.5 when approximating a discrete variable with a continuous one?'

discoveryHook.scenario: A binomial distribution uses bars with width 1. A normal curve is continuous. To match them, we extend each discrete value by half a unit on each side. This 'continuity correction' ensures the area under the normal curve matches the binomial probability more accurately.

explanation: The [[kw:continuity correction]] adjusts a discrete binomial interval to a continuous normal interval by adding or subtracting 0.5.
For $P(x \ge c)$ (at least c), use $x > c - 0.5$.
For $P(x \le c)$ (at most c), use $x < c + 0.5$.
For $P(x = c)$ (exactly c), use $c - 0.5 < x < c + 0.5$.
For intervals like 'between a and b inclusive', use $a - 0.5 < x < b + 0.5$.

formulaCard.title: Continuity Correction Rule
notes: Add 0.5 to upper bound for ≤ or <.
Subtract 0.5 from lower bound for ≥ or >.

examples.title: A – Inclusive Interval
examples.prompt: Convert the binomial probability of getting between 270 and 310 successes inclusive to a normal distribution interval.
steps: Include 0.5 below the lowest and 0.5 above the highest.

examples.title: B – At Least
examples.prompt: Convert the binomial probability of getting at least 158 successes to a normal distribution interval.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why do you subtract 0.5 from 158 instead of adding?
steps: The lower bound is 158, so subtract 0.5 to include the entire bar for 158.

examples.title: C – Fewer Than
examples.prompt: Convert the binomial probability of getting fewer than 63 successes to a normal distribution interval.
steps: The highest integer included is 62, so add 0.5.

confusionCorner.title: Direction of Correction
confusionCorner.body: For 'at least', subtract 0.5 from the lower bound. For 'at most' or 'fewer than', add 0.5 to the upper bound. Getting the direction wrong reverses the inequality.

questions.prompt: When approximating a binomial probability with a normal distribution, you apply a ___ correction by adding or subtracting 0.5.
hints: It adjusts for the discrete nature of the binomial.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: It is called a continuity correction.

questions.prompt: For the binomial probability $P(x \le 109)$, what normal interval should you use?
For the binomial probability $P(x > 109)$, what normal interval should you use?

blocks.title: Approximating Binomial Probabilities
teacherCues: Walk through the steps: verify conditions, compute μ and σ, apply continuity correction, find z-score, use table.
Use Example 3 (fewer than 20 respond yes) to illustrate the full process.

discoveryHook.scenario: With the normal approximation, a binomial probability that would require summing many terms becomes a simple matter of finding a z-score and looking up an area. This is the power of the Central Limit Theorem applied to binomial data.

explanation: To approximate a binomial probability using a normal distribution, follow these steps.
1. Verify $ n p \ge 5 $ and $ n q \ge 5 $.
2. Compute the mean $ \mu = n p $ and standard deviation $ \sigma = \sqrt{n p q} $.
3. Apply the continuity correction to rewrite the probability in terms of a normal interval.
4. Convert the boundary to a z-score using $ z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma} $.
5. Use the standard normal table to find the probability.

formulaCard.title: Z-Score for Normal Approximation
notes: σ is the standard deviation of the binomial distribution.

examples.title: A – Fewer Than 20 Respond Yes
examples.prompt: Sixty-two percent of adults have an HDTV. You select 45 adults. Find the probability that fewer than 20 respond yes.
steps: From earlier, $\mu = 27.9$, $\sigma \approx 3.26$. Normal approximation is valid.
Table area left of -2.58 is 0.0049. So probability ≈ 0.0049.

examples.title: B – At Least 120 Never Wear Helmet
examples.prompt: Fifty-eight percent of adults never wear a helmet when riding. You select 200 adults. Find the probability that at least 120 say they never wear a helmet.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why do you use 119.5 instead of 120 in the z-score?

examples.title: C – More Than 9 Respond Yes
examples.prompt: Five percent of adults plan to buy a 3D TV. You select 125 adults. Find the probability that more than 9 respond yes.

confusionCorner.title: Continuity Correction Before Z-Score
confusionCorner.body: Always apply the continuity correction before computing the z-score. If you skip it, the probability may be noticeably off, especially for small to moderate n.

questions.prompt: In the normal approximation, the z-score formula uses the ___ of the binomial distribution in the denominator.
hints: Not the standard error; this is a single sample of counts.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: The denominator is the standard deviation $\sigma = \sqrt{npq}$.

questions.prompt: For $n=45$, $p=0.62$, $\mu=27.9$, $\sigma=3.26$, and continuity-corrected x=19.5, what is the z-score? Round to two decimal places.
If the area to the left of z = -2.58 is 0.0049, what is the probability that fewer than 20 respond yes?
hints: The table gives the cumulative area directly.

blocks.title: Approximating 'Exactly' Probabilities
teacherCues: Explain that for P(x = c), the continuity interval is c−0.5 to c+0.5.
Use Example 5 with exactly 96 to show two z-scores and subtract areas.

discoveryHook.scenario: What if you need the probability of exactly 96 successes? The normal approximation treats this as the area under the curve between 95.5 and 96.5. Two z-scores and a subtraction give the answer—far faster than the binomial formula for large n.

explanation: To approximate $P(x = c)$ with a normal distribution, use the continuity interval $c - 0.5 < x < c + 0.5$.
Find the z-score for $c - 0.5$ and for $c + 0.5$.
The probability is the difference of the two cumulative areas.
This works because for a continuous distribution, the probability of an interval equals the area under the curve over that interval.
Remember: $P(x = c) \approx P(c - 0.5 < x < c + 0.5)$.

examples.title: A – Exactly 96 Use Internet Explorer
examples.prompt: Sixty-two percent of Internet users use Internet Explorer. You select 150 users. Find the probability that exactly 96 say yes.

examples.title: B – Exactly 27 Use Firefox
examples.prompt: Twenty-four percent of Internet users use Firefox. You select 150 users. Find the probability that exactly 27 say yes.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why do you need two z-scores for an 'exactly' probability?

examples.title: C – Exactly 50 Use Internet
examples.prompt: Seventy percent of adults ages 50-64 use the Internet. You select 80 adults. Find the probability that exactly 50 say yes.

confusionCorner.title: Exact vs. At Least
confusionCorner.body: For 'exactly c', use the interval (c−0.5, c+0.5). For 'at least c', use x > c−0.5. The two are different and require different boundaries.

questions.prompt: To approximate $P(x = c)$ with a normal distribution, use the interval $c - 0.5 < x < c + $ ___.
hints: It is half a unit above c.
The interval is symmetric around c.

questions.prompt: For $\mu = 93$, $\sigma = 5.94$, what is the z-score for $x = 95.5$? Round to two decimal places.
If the areas for z = 0.42 and z = 0.59 are 0.6628 and 0.7224, what is the probability of exactly 96 successes?
hints: Subtract the smaller area from the larger area.

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid – Solving Normal Approximation Problems
teacherCues: Display Understand → Solve → Conclude. Walk through a full binomial approximation problem, e.g., at most 75 favorite sport.
Emphasize: Understand verifies conditions; Solve applies continuity correction and z-score; Conclude interprets probability.

discoveryHook.scenario: The blueprint keeps you organized when approximating binomial probabilities. Understand the problem and check conditions, Solve with mean, standard deviation, continuity correction, and z-scores, then Conclude with the probability and its meaning.

explanation: [[imp:Understand]] – Read the problem. Identify n, p, q. Verify $ n p \ge 5 $ and $ n q \ge 5 $. Determine the type of probability (≤, ≥, <, >, =) and the required continuity correction.
[[imp:Solve]] – Compute $ \mu = n p $ and $ \sigma = \sqrt{n p q} $. Apply the continuity correction. Find z-score(s). Use the standard normal table to find the probability.
[[imp:Conclude]] – State the probability. Determine if unusual (< 0.05). Interpret in context.

rows.1: Identify n, p, q; check conditions; determine continuity correction.
Compute μ and σ; find z; use table.

formulaCard.title: Key Formulas
notes: For exactly c, use two z-scores.

examples.title: A – Full Blueprint: At Most 75
examples.prompt: Use blueprint: 35% of adults say favorite sport is football. You select 150 adults. Find probability at most 75 say yes.
steps: Understand: $n=150$, $p=0.35$, $q=0.65$. Check $np=52.5$, $nq=97.5$; both ≥5. At most 75 includes 75, so continuity correction $x < 75.5$.

examples.title: B – Full Blueprint: More Than 40
examples.prompt: Using same data, find probability more than 40 say yes.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why do we use 40.5 instead of 40?
steps: Understand: More than 40 means x > 40, continuity correction x > 40.5.

examples.title: C – Decide and Compute
examples.prompt: Use blueprint: 34% of workers are college graduates. You select 50 workers. Find probability that more than 23 are graduates.
steps: Understand: $n=50$, $p=0.34$, $q=0.66$. Check $np=17$, $nq=33$; both ≥5. More than 23 means x > 23.5.

confusionCorner.title: Continuity Correction Direction
confusionCorner.body: Always confirm the direction: at most includes the endpoint, so add 0.5; more than excludes the endpoint, so add 0.5; at least includes, so subtract 0.5; fewer than excludes, so subtract 0.5. If unsure, list the integers included.

questions.prompt: In the Understand phase, what two products must be at least 5?
hints: They involve n, p, and q.
The conditions are np ≥ 5 and nq ≥ 5.

questions.prompt: In the Solve phase, apply the continuity correction, then compute the ___ using $z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$.
If a probability is 0.0268, is the event unusual? (yes/no)

presenterNotes: Start by motivating why a normal approximation is needed for large n. Use a histogram of binomial distributions for different n to show convergence to normal.
Drill the conditions np ≥ 5 and nq ≥ 5. Emphasize both must hold.
The continuity correction is the trickiest part. Use visual aids with bars and curves to show why 0.5 is added or subtracted.
Practice all forms: ≤, ≥, <, >, =. Students often confuse the direction of the correction.
The blueprint helps structure multi-step problems. Encourage students to always verify conditions first.
